plan.contextChunk: This figure contains two panels, (a) and (b), showing the same Fibonacci heap H in two complementary representations. Panel (a) uses an abstract tree view: five min-heap-ordered trees share a circular root list whose five root nodes — 23, 7, 3, 17, and 24 — are connected by a horizontal dashed line; an H.min pointer above points down to the minimum root node 3. The tree rooted at 3 has three children: 18, 52, and 38; node 18 has one child 39, and node 38 has one child 41. The tree rooted at 24 has children 26 and 46, where 26 has one child 35. The tree rooted at 17 has one child 30. Nodes 18, 39, and 26 are drawn as filled black circles with white numerals, indicating they are marked. Panel (b) shows the same heap with an explicit pointer diagram: each node is still a circular node and both the root list and each sibling list of children are represented as circular doubly linked lists with pairs of directed arrows indicating forward and backward pointers. The H.min pointer and the marked nodes (18, 39, 26) are identical to those in panel (a). This figure establishes the two-level representation of a Fibonacci heap, contrasting the abstract tree view with the concrete pointer structure, and identifies marked nodes as those that have lost one child since last becoming a root.

interactionPlan.concept: A Fibonacci heap is a circular doubly linked list of min-heap-ordered trees; the abstract tree picture and the explicit pointer picture describe the same structure, and the pointer view is what makes insertion O(1).

interactions.label: Representation
interactions.teaches: The tidy tree drawing and the tangle of arrows are the same heap; the dashed root line and the parent-child edges are shorthand for circular doubly linked lists and parent/child pointers.
Every node stores exactly four pointers — p, child, left, right — and in a sibling list of size one the left and right pointers point back at the node itself.

interactions.label: FIB-HEAP-INSERT(H, 21)
interactions.teaches: Insertion only relinks a constant number of pointers in the root list and compares one key against H.min — no tree restructuring, so it costs O(1).

demo_steps.title: The abstract view
demo_steps.narration: Five min-heap-ordered trees sit in a root list, drawn as a dashed line; H.min points at the smallest root, 3. Each tree obeys the heap property, but nothing constrains the trees' shapes relative to one another.

demo_steps.title: Marked nodes
demo_steps.narration: Nodes 18, 39, and 26 are black: each has lost one child since it last became the child of another node. A second loss would cut it into the root list.

demo_steps.title: The same heap, in pointers
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the pointer view: the dashed root line becomes a circular doubly linked list, and every set of siblings gets its own circular list. Click any node to light up its parent, child, left, and right pointers.

demo_steps.title: Why circular and doubly linked
demo_steps.narration: Click node 30 or 35: a lone child's left and right pointers loop back to itself. Circular lists mean splicing a node in or out touches only a fixed number of pointers, with no head or tail special cases.

demo_steps.title: Insert key 21
demo_steps.narration: Create a single-node tree holding 21 and splice it into the root list between two existing roots by rewiring four pointers.

demo_steps.title: Check H.min
demo_steps.narration: Compare 21 against H.min's key 3. Since 21 > 3, H.min stays on 3. The whole operation was a constant number of pointer writes and one comparison — O(1), with no consolidation.

demo_steps.title: Back to the abstract picture
demo_steps.narration: Return to the tree view: the heap now has six roots. The lazy, unconsolidated root list is exactly what buys Fibonacci heaps their fast inserts and decrease-keys.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Because the root list and every sibling list are circular and doubly linked, adding a tree is just four pointer assignments and one key comparison — the heap stays deliberately messy so that insertion costs O(1).
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Two stacked panels sharing identical node positions. Nodes are circles ~28px radius: unmarked = light gray fill, thin black stroke, black numeral; marked (18, 39, 26) = solid black fill, white bold numeral. Panel (a): five roots evenly spread across the top on one horizontal line (23, 7, 3, 17, 24) joined by a black dashed line; H.min rendered as italic serif text above node 3 with a short downward arrow. Solid thin edges descend from 3 to its three children (18, 52, 38 spread beneath it), from 18 to 39, from 38 to 41, from 17 to 30, from 24 to 26 and 46, and from 26 to 35. Depth increases downward in three levels. Panel (b): same node coordinates, but each sibling group is wrapped in a rounded 'racetrack' rail — one rail above the group carrying rightward arrows, one below carrying leftward arrows, with the rails curving around the outermost nodes to close the cycle. Singleton lists (30, 39, 41, 35) get small self-loop rails above and below. Between a parent and its leftmost-drawn child, draw a pair of parallel vertical arrows in opposite directions (child→parent for p, parent→child for child pointer); other children connect to the parent only via the sibling rail. Use a single accent color (e.g. orange) for click-highlighted pointers with small italic labels p / child / left / right, and a second accent (e.g. green) for the newly inserted node 21 and its dashed splice arrows. Keep the layout wide and airy; the visual contrast between the calm dashed line of (a) and the dense arrow lattice of (b) is the point.

authoredContext: (a) A Fibonacci heap consisting of five min-heap-ordered trees and 14 nodes. The dashed line indicates the root list. The minimum node of the heap is the node containing the key 3. Black nodes are marked. The potential of this particular Fibonacci heap is 5C2_x0001_ 3 D 11. (b) A more complete representation showing pointers p (up arrows), child (down arrows), and left and right (sideways arrows). The remaining figures in this chapter omit these details, since all the information shown here can be determined from what appears in part (a).

discrepancies: Panel (b) is vertically compressed relative to the source: the three node rows (713/883/1053) sit closer together than in the printed figure, so the circular-list rails hug the nodes tightly and the parent/child arrow pairs are very short, making the two-arrow (p and child) pairs hard to distinguish at inline size.

In the source, each sibling list's return rail is a clearly separated rounded loop below the row with a visible arrowhead entering the leftmost node; in the render the forward/return rails of the root list nearly merge into a single band at default zoom, reducing the 'circular doubly linked' read that is the whole point of panel (b).

Green 'key 21' insertion overlay, annotation text ('O(1): 4 pointer writes', '21 > 3 ⇒ H.min unchanged') and the legend swatch are additions not present in the source figure — correct CLRS content but extra chrome; they are hidden at step 0, so impact is limited.

Node glyphs in the generated figure read smaller relative to the canvas than in the source (where circles dominate the composition), so the two-digit keys are noticeably less prominent at inline size.
evaluation.notes: Accurate reproduction of CLRS Fig 19.1 in both panels with correct node keys, tree topology, marked (black) nodes, dashed root list, H.min arrows and panel letters, backed by genuinely useful interactions (panel toggle, per-node p/child/left/right pointer highlighting, insert-phase stepper, 7-step guided demo); main weaknesses are the vertically compressed panel (b) where the circular-list rails and parent/child arrow pairs crowd together, and small node/key type at inline size.
action_items: Increase vertical separation between the panel (b) rows (fbRowB) and/or the rail offsets (yF/yB, rt/rb) so the forward and return rails are visibly distinct loops and the paired p/child arrows between levels are clearly two separate arrows, as in the source.
Enlarge node radius / key font slightly (or reduce viewbox width padding) so the circles and two-digit keys carry the same visual weight they do in the printed figure at inline size.

Add small static 'left/right/p/child' callouts on one representative sibling list (or keep them visible after a hover) so the pointer semantics are legible without requiring a click, and ensure the orange pointer labels do not sit on top of adjacent rails when a dense node like 3 is selected.
Dim or visually separate the green insertion overlay text so it never overlaps the black pointer arrows in panel (b) at the 'spliced' and 'H.min updated' phases.

feedback.rationale: Concept, panels, and interaction structure are correct; remaining issues are concrete rendering fixes (row spacing, rail separation, node/key sizing, label overlap) that belong to the generator.

discrepancies: Panel (b) adds gray italic pointer callouts ('right', 'left', 'p', 'child') that do not exist in the source; they render at roughly 7–8 px at inline size and are essentially unreadable, so they read as clutter rather than annotation.

In the 'new node created' phase (demo step / dropdown), the green 21 node is placed at y≈62 in panel (a) and y≈568 in panel (b), overlapping the H.min arrow shaft and the italic 'H.min' caption respectively — a label/artwork collision the source never has.

Primary captions ('H.min', '(a)', '(b)') are proportionally smaller relative to the node keys than in the source, where H.min and the panel letters are visually dominant; the generated hierarchy is flatter.

The insertion of key 21 (green node, green splice arrows, 'O(1): 4 pointer writes' plates) is entirely absent from the source figure — acceptable as a teaching overlay, but it changes the default look once a phase other than 'before' is selected.
evaluation.notes: Structurally a near drop-in replacement for CLRS Fig. 19.2 — both panels, correct root list, sibling rails, p/child pairs, and marked black nodes — with rich, genuinely pedagogical interactions (panel toggle, insert phases, node-click pointer highlight, 7-step demo), let down mainly by illegibly small added pointer callouts and a couple of overlay/label collisions during the insert phases.

Move the step-1 'new node created' green circle (and its self-loop rails) clear of the H.min arrow in panel (a) and of the 'H.min' caption in panel (b) — e.g. offset it below/right of the arrow or shift the H.min glyph.

Re-check the explanatory plates ('O(1): 4 pointer writes', '21 > 3 ⇒ H.min unchanged') for overlap with the root-list rails and tree edges at all viewport widths; anchor them in a dedicated empty band instead of fixed absolute coordinates.

Consider hiding the added green insert overlay whenever the user is on the 'before' phase in both dropdown and demo so the default state is pixel-faithful to the printed figure (already true at step 0 — keep it that way when switching views).

feedback.rationale: The conceptual decomposition and interaction structure are correct; the remaining issues are implementation-level fixes to font sizes, label hierarchy, and overlay collision placement.

plan.concept: A Fibonacci heap is a circular doubly linked list of min-heap-ordered trees; the abstract tree picture and the explicit pointer picture describe the same structure, and the pointer view is what makes insertion O(1).

interactions.label: Representation
interactions.teaches: The tidy tree drawing and the tangle of arrows are the same heap; the dashed root line and the parent-child edges are shorthand for circular doubly linked lists and parent/child pointers.
Every node stores exactly four pointers — p, child, left, right — and in a sibling list of size one the left and right pointers point back at the node itself.

interactions.label: FIB-HEAP-INSERT(H, 21)
interactions.teaches: Insertion only relinks a constant number of pointers in the root list and compares one key against H.min — no tree restructuring, so it costs O(1).

demo_steps.title: The abstract view
demo_steps.narration: Five min-heap-ordered trees sit in a root list, drawn as a dashed line; H.min points at the smallest root, 3. Each tree obeys the heap property, but nothing constrains the trees' shapes relative to one another.

demo_steps.title: Marked nodes
demo_steps.narration: Nodes 18, 39, and 26 are black: each has lost one child since it last became the child of another node. A second loss would cut it into the root list.

demo_steps.title: The same heap, in pointers
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the pointer view: the dashed root line becomes a circular doubly linked list, and every set of siblings gets its own circular list. Click any node to light up its parent, child, left, and right pointers.

demo_steps.title: Why circular and doubly linked
demo_steps.narration: Click node 30 or 35: a lone child's left and right pointers loop back to itself. Circular lists mean splicing a node in or out touches only a fixed number of pointers, with no head or tail special cases.

demo_steps.title: Insert key 21
demo_steps.narration: Create a single-node tree holding 21 and splice it into the root list between two existing roots by rewiring four pointers.

demo_steps.title: Check H.min
demo_steps.narration: Compare 21 against H.min's key 3. Since 21 > 3, H.min stays on 3. The whole operation was a constant number of pointer writes and one comparison — O(1), with no consolidation.

demo_steps.title: Back to the abstract picture
demo_steps.narration: Return to the tree view: the heap now has six roots. The lazy, unconsolidated root list is exactly what buys Fibonacci heaps their fast inserts and decrease-keys.

plan.keyInsight: Because the root list and every sibling list are circular and doubly linked, adding a tree is just four pointer assignments and one key comparison — the heap stays deliberately messy so that insertion costs O(1).
plan.reconstructionNotes: Two stacked panels sharing identical node positions. Nodes are circles ~28px radius: unmarked = light gray fill, thin black stroke, black numeral; marked (18, 39, 26) = solid black fill, white bold numeral. Panel (a): five roots evenly spread across the top on one horizontal line (23, 7, 3, 17, 24) joined by a black dashed line; H.min rendered as italic serif text above node 3 with a short downward arrow. Solid thin edges descend from 3 to its three children (18, 52, 38 spread beneath it), from 18 to 39, from 38 to 41, from 17 to 30, from 24 to 26 and 46, and from 26 to 35. Depth increases downward in three levels. Panel (b): same node coordinates, but each sibling group is wrapped in a rounded 'racetrack' rail — one rail above the group carrying rightward arrows, one below carrying leftward arrows, with the rails curving around the outermost nodes to close the cycle. Singleton lists (30, 39, 41, 35) get small self-loop rails above and below. Between a parent and its leftmost-drawn child, draw a pair of parallel vertical arrows in opposite directions (child→parent for p, parent→child for child pointer); other children connect to the parent only via the sibling rail. Use a single accent color (e.g. orange) for click-highlighted pointers with small italic labels p / child / left / right, and a second accent (e.g. green) for the newly inserted node 21 and its dashed splice arrows. Keep the layout wide and airy; the visual contrast between the calm dashed line of (a) and the dense arrow lattice of (b) is the point.
